analogy.p: Think of volume as how much sand a solid can hold, and surface area as how much wrapping paper you need to cover it. A cone shows the 'one third' rule beautifully: if you fill a cone-shaped paper cup with sand and pour it into a cylinder with the same radius and height, you need exactly three cones to fill the cylinder, so V = ⅓πr²h. The analogy breaks down because real paper cups have a rim and thickness, whereas the maths solid is a perfect shape with no thickness, so volume and surface area are exact.

bullets: **Volume** is the amount of space inside a 3D shape. It is measured in cubic units such as cm³, m³ or mm³.
**Surface area** is the total area of all the faces (or the curved surface plus flat faces) added together. It is measured in square units such as cm² or m².
**Capacity** means how much liquid a container holds. 1 litre = 1000 cm³ and 1 millilitre = 1 cm³.

You must know by heart: the volume of a prism, cylinder and pyramid, and the surface area of a cylinder. The Edexcel formula sheet gives the volume and surface area of a sphere and the volume and curved surface area of a cone (check your own copy before the exam).
Questions are on all three papers; Paper 1 (non-calculator) usually wants answers **in terms of π**.
Command words: 'work out', 'calculate', 'show that', 'find the exact value', 'give your answer in terms of π'. Each one tells you what form of answer earns the accuracy mark.
core.p: Edexcel 1MA1 (strands G16 and G17) expects you to know and apply the formulae for the **volume** and **surface area** of cuboids, prisms, cylinders, **pyramids**, **cones** and **spheres**, and to combine them for **composite solids** such as a cone on top of a hemisphere. At Higher tier you must also cope with **frustums** (a cone with its top cut off), solids with parts removed (for example a hemispherical bowl hollowed from a cylinder), and problems that ask you to work backwards from a given volume to a missing length. The skill is not just substituting numbers: it is choosing the right formula, finding any hidden length (usually with **Pythagoras**), and presenting the answer with sensible units and rounding.

bullets: Length: cm. Area: cm² (length × length). Volume: cm³ (length × length × length).
Converting length units: 1 m = 100 cm, 1 cm = 10 mm.
Converting area units: 1 m² = 100 × 100 = **10 000 cm²** and 1 cm² = 10 × 10 = **100 mm²**. You square the length conversion factor.
Converting volume units: 1 m³ = 100 × 100 × 100 = **1 000 000 cm³** and 1 cm³ = 10 × 10 × 10 = **1000 mm³**. You cube the length conversion factor.
1 litre = 1000 cm³ = 0.001 m³. So 1 m³ = 1000 litres.
Always write units on the final answer; method marks are not lost for missing units in the working, but the final accuracy mark usually requires them.
Sense check: a larger answer for volume than expected usually means you used diameter instead of radius, or forgot the one third.
core.h: Volume versus surface area and getting units right
core.p: Volume counts how many unit cubes fit inside a solid, while surface area counts how many unit squares are needed to cover the outside. Because they measure different things, they have different units, and the examiner will not give the final accuracy mark if you write cm² for a volume. When a question mixes units (for example a radius in metres and a height in centimetres) you must convert everything to one unit **before** substituting, because squaring or cubing a mixed-unit number gives nonsense.

bullets: **Volume of a prism = area of cross-section × length.** This works for triangular prisms, trapeziums, L-shapes, anything with a constant cross-section.
**Volume of a cylinder = πr²h**, where r is the radius and h is the height (length).
**Curved surface area of a cylinder = 2πrh** (the rectangle is 2πr wide by h tall).
**Total surface area of a closed cylinder = 2πrh + 2πr²** (curved surface plus two circular ends).
For an open cylinder (like a cup or a tube with one end missing) include only the circles that are really there; read the question for 'open' or 'closed'.

For a triangular prism, total surface area = 2 × triangle area + the three rectangles. If the triangle is right-angled you may need Pythagoras for the hypotenuse side before finding the third rectangle.
If a cross-section is composite (for example a rectangle with a semicircle on top), find its area first, then multiply by the length.
core.p: A **prism** is a solid with the same cross-section all the way through. Its volume is the area of the cross-section multiplied by the length (or height) of the prism, because you are stacking identical layers. A **cylinder** is a circular prism, so the cross-section is a circle of area πr² and the volume is πr²h. The surface area of any prism is found by adding the areas of every face; for a cylinder the curved surface unrolls into a rectangle whose width is the circumference of the circle.

bullets: **Volume of a pyramid = ⅓ × area of base × perpendicular height.** The base can be a square, rectangle, triangle or any polygon.
The **perpendicular height** is at right angles to the base; it is not the sloping edge or the slant height of a face.
**Surface area of a pyramid = area of base + area of all the triangular faces.** Each triangular face = ½ × base edge × slant height of that face.

For a square-based pyramid with a vertical apex over the centre, the slant height l satisfies l² = h² + (a/2)², where a is the side of the base. Draw this right-angled triangle separately: its legs are the height h and half the base side, and its hypotenuse is the slant height.
The sloping **edge** (from a base corner to the apex) is longer than the slant height. It uses half the base **diagonal**: edge² = h² + (d/2)², where d = a√2 for a square.
Tetrahedron and other pyramids: base area may need a triangle formula (½ab sin C) first.
Common exam move: the question gives the slant edge length, you find the vertical height with Pythagoras, then use the ⅓ formula.
core.p: A **pyramid** has a polygon as its base and triangular faces that meet at a single point called the **apex**. Its volume is exactly **one third** of the volume of the prism with the same base and the same perpendicular height, which is why the formula has a ⅓ in it. The key difficulty with pyramids is that there are two different heights: the **perpendicular (vertical) height** goes straight up from the centre of the base to the apex and is used in the volume formula, whereas the **slant height** runs up the middle of a triangular face and is used when finding the area of that face.

bullets: **Volume of a cone = ⅓πr²h.** Given on the formula sheet, but you should recognise it as one third of the cylinder formula.
**Slant height: l² = r² + h²**, so l = √(r² + h²). This is Pythagoras applied to the cross-section through the apex.
If a question gives l and r, find h = √(l² − r²) before using the volume formula.
Common right-angled triples help on the non-calculator paper: (3, 4, 5), (5, 12, 13), (8, 15, 17) and multiples.
Three cones of the same radius and height fill one cylinder: the 'one third' is why a cone holds less than it looks like it should.
When answers are required 'in terms of π', leave π in the answer and do all other arithmetic exactly (for example ⅓ × π × 25 × 12 = 100π).
A cone with r = 5 and h = 12 has l = 13 and V = ⅓ × π × 25 × 12 = 100π ≈ 314.2 cm³.
core.h: Cones: volume and the role of slant height
core.p: A **cone** is a pyramid whose base is a circle. Its volume is therefore ⅓ × base area × perpendicular height, giving **V = ⅓πr²h**. Just as for the pyramid, the volume formula uses the **perpendicular height h** (from the apex straight down to the centre of the circular base). The **slant height l** is the distance from the apex down the side to the edge of the base, and it forms the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle with the radius r and the perpendicular height h, so l² = r² + h². A cone is exactly one third of the cylinder with the same radius and height.

bullets: **Curved surface area (CSA) of a cone = πrl**, where l is the slant height (not the vertical height).
**Total surface area of a cone = πrl + πr²** (curved surface plus circular base).
If the question says 'an open cone' or 'a conical hat' there is no base, so only πrl is needed.
The sector angle of the net is θ = (r/l) × 360° (Higher tier extension, and useful for 'design a cone from a sector' questions).
Because the arc length of the sector equals the base circumference: (θ/360) × 2πl = 2πr.
Mark scheme language: 'uses slant height 13 (Pythagoras)', then 'π × 5 × 13', then the answer with units.
core.h: Cones: curved surface area and total surface area
core.p: If you cut a cone along its slant edge and unroll it, the curved surface becomes a **sector of a circle** whose radius is the slant height l. The arc of this sector is the circumference of the circular base, 2πr. Since the sector is the fraction (2πr)/(2πl) = r/l of a full circle of radius l, its area is (r/l) × πl² = **πrl**. This is where the formula for the **curved surface area of a cone** comes from. A total surface area includes the circular base as well.

bullets: **Sphere: V = 4/3 πr³; surface area = 4πr².**
**Hemisphere: V = ⅔πr³; curved surface area = 2πr²; total surface area (solid) = 2πr² + πr² = 3πr².**
Sphere volume is cubed in r, so doubling the radius makes the volume 8 times larger and the surface area 4 times larger (links to area and volume scale factors).
If the question gives the **diameter**, halve it first. A ball of diameter 12 cm has r = 6 cm and V = 4/3 × π × 216 = 288π cm³.
Working backwards: if V = 288π then 4/3 r³ = 288, so r³ = 216 and r = 6. Use the cube root key or recognise perfect cubes (8, 27, 64, 125, 216).

A hemispherical bowl 'of radius r' holds ⅔πr³ if filled to the brim; the outer and inner surfaces are different sizes if the bowl has thickness, so subtract inner from outer volume to get the volume of material.
For exact answers keep fractions: ⅔ × π × 27 = 18π.
core.p: A **sphere** is perfectly round: every point on its surface is the same distance, the radius r, from the centre. Its volume is **V = 4/3 πr³** and its surface area is **A = 4πr²**; both are on the formula sheet. A **hemisphere** is half a sphere, so its volume is half: ⅔πr³. Its curved surface is half of 4πr², which is 2πr², and if the question asks for the **total** surface area of a solid hemisphere you must also add the flat circular face πr², making 3πr².

bullets: **Total volume = sum of the volumes** of the parts (or whole minus hollowed-out part).
**Surface area = only the exposed surfaces.** When a cone sits on a hemisphere of the same radius, the circular base of the cone and the flat face of the hemisphere are joined and are not counted.
Example: cone (r = 3, h = 4, l = 5) on hemisphere (r = 3): V = ⅓π(9)(4) + ⅔π(27) = 12π + 18π = 30π ≈ 94.2 cm³.
Same solid, surface area = πrl + 2πr² = 15π + 18π = 33π ≈ 103.7 cm².
A capsule (cylinder with a hemisphere on each end): V = πr²h + 4/3πr³ (two hemispheres make a whole sphere), and surface area = 2πrh + 4πr².
Take care with heights: if the total height of the solid is given, subtract the radius of the hemisphere (and any other parts) to find the height of the cylinder or cone part.
If the shape has a hole or cavity, subtract the volume of the hole; for surface area you may need to add the inside surface of the hole.
Always make a short list: 'Part 1: ..., Part 2: ...' with the dimensions of each part written beside it.
core.p: A **composite solid** is built by joining simple solids, for example a cone on a hemisphere or a cylinder with a hemisphere on each end (a capsule). To find the volume you add the volumes of the parts (or subtract a part that has been removed). To find the surface area you add only the surfaces that are still **on the outside**: the faces where two parts are glued together are hidden and must **not** be counted. Always sketch the solid, list the parts and decide which faces are exposed before you calculate.

bullets: **Volume of frustum = volume of large cone − volume of small cone.**
The large and small cones are similar: r_small / r_large = h_small / h_large.
If you are told the frustum's height, the unknown height of the small cone is found by forming an equation: e.g. h/(h + 10) = 6/12 gives h = 10.
Worked example: large cone r = 12, h = 20, small cone cut off has r = 6, h = 10. V = ⅓π(144)(20) − ⅓π(36)(10) = 960π − 120π = 840π ≈ 2639 cm³.
Surface area of a frustum = curved surface of large cone − curved surface of small cone + area of the base circle + area of the top circle.
The curved part of a frustum is NOT πrl for any single r and l; you must subtract: π R L − π r l, where L and l are the slant heights of the large and small cones.
Drawing a labelled cross-section (a trapezium with dashed lines extended to the apex) makes the similar triangles obvious.
core.p: A **frustum** is what remains when a small cone is cut off the top of a larger cone by a plane parallel to the base. You find its volume by **subtraction**: volume of the original (large) cone minus volume of the small cone that was removed. The two cones are **similar**, so their lengths are in the same ratio, and this lets you find the missing height or radius of the small cone using similar triangles. This is a typical 4 to 5 mark Higher question because it combines the cone formula with similarity.

bullets: Cylinder: V = πr²h gives r = √(V ÷ (πh)) and h = V ÷ (πr²).
Cone: V = ⅓πr²h gives h = 3V ÷ (πr²) and r = √(3V ÷ (πh)).
Sphere: V = 4/3πr³ gives r = ∛(3V ÷ 4π).
Equal volumes: a cone (r = 6, h = 8) melted into a sphere: ⅓π(36)(8) = 96π = 4/3πR³, so R³ = 72 and R = ∛72 ≈ 4.16 cm.
Algebraic dimensions: if the radius is x and the height is 2x, then V = πx²(2x) = 2πx³ and you can solve for x.
Do not round until the final step; use the calculator's ANS or store values to keep accuracy.
Give the answer to 3 significant figures unless told otherwise, and state units.
core.p: Many Higher questions give you the volume (or surface area) and ask for a missing length, or give two solids with equal volumes and ask for a radius or height. The method is to write the volume formula with the known numbers substituted, then **rearrange** to isolate the unknown, taking a square root or cube root at the end. For equal-volume problems (for example a cone of clay reshaped into a sphere), set the two volume expressions equal and solve; the π cancels on both sides, which makes the algebra simpler.

bullets: **Density = mass ÷ volume**, so mass = density × volume and volume = mass ÷ density. Units: g/cm³ with mass in g and volume in cm³.
Capacity: litres to cm³ is × 1000; cm³ to litres is ÷ 1000.
Flow rate: time = volume ÷ rate. Example: a 3000 cm³ tank filled at 250 cm³ per second takes 12 seconds.
Water level rise: the added volume equals area of the surface × rise in height. For a cylinder of radius r, rise = added volume ÷ πr².
A solid dropped into water raises the level by volume of solid ÷ cross-sectional area of the container.
Filling a conical funnel or inverted cone: the surface of the liquid is a smaller similar cone, so use similar triangles for its radius.
Cost problems: paint cost = surface area × cost per cm² (or per m²), so convert surface area units before multiplying.
core.h: Capacity, density, flow rate and changing water level
core.p: Real-world 3D measure problems nearly always combine volume with another quantity. **Density** links mass and volume (density = mass ÷ volume), **flow rate** links volume and time, and a **water level problem** asks how high liquid rises in a container when a volume is added. In every case your first step is to calculate a volume, then convert units if needed, then use the second relationship.

bullets: Keep π throughout: ⅓ × π × 6² × 8 = ⅓ × 36 × 8 × π = 96π.
Cancel before multiplying: 4/3 × π × 27 = 4 × 9 × π = 36π.
Check you used radius not diameter before simplifying.
Surds may appear: slant height of a cone with r = 3, h = 6 is l = √45 = 3√5, so CSA = π × 3 × 3√5 = 9√5π.
Rounding: 3 s.f. is the default for non-exact answers; never round intermediate lengths (use the full calculator value).
Using π ≈ 3.14 when the question tells you to use the π button can lose the accuracy mark.
A good habit: write the exact form first, then the decimal, e.g. 100π = 314.159... = 314 cm³ (3 s.f.).
core.h: Exact answers, non-calculator technique and rounding
core.p: On Paper 1 you have no calculator, so Edexcel often says 'leave your answer in terms of π' or 'give your answer as an exact value'. This means the final answer should look like 96π cm³ or 12π√2. You keep π as a symbol, multiply and simplify the other numbers, and do not convert to a decimal. On Papers 2 and 3 you will usually be asked for a decimal answer to a given accuracy, so you use the π button and round only at the end.

bullets: Learn: volume of a prism, cylinder (πr²h), cuboid, and pyramid (⅓ × base × height).
Learn: surface area of a cylinder and of cuboids/prisms (add face areas).
Given: volume of a cone ⅓πr²h, curved surface area of a cone πrl, volume of a sphere 4/3πr³ and surface area of a sphere 4πr² (check your sheet).
Derive when needed: hemisphere = half sphere; total SA of a solid hemisphere adds the flat circle (3πr²).
Know Pythagoras (a² + b² = c²) and basic trigonometry because many 3D measure questions need them for a hidden length.
Know area formulae: triangle ½bh, trapezium ½(a + b)h, circle πr².
Know how to find a sector area and arc length (previous topic) because cones link to sectors.
core.h: Which formulae to learn and which are given
core.p: Edexcel provides some formulae on the Higher formulae page but not others, and mark schemes assume you know the rest. Learn the table below so that you never waste time. Note that formulae on the sheet are only useful if you can identify what each letter stands for; in particular l is the slant height of a cone, not the vertical height.

bullets: Similarity: if lengths scale by k, areas scale by k² and volumes scale by k³. Use this to avoid calculating two volumes separately.
Trigonometry: if the angle between a slant edge and the base is given, h = l sin θ and the base radius = l cos θ.
Circle theorems and sectors: net of a cone is a sector; arc length = base circumference.
Algebra: forming and solving an equation such as ⅓π(x)²(3x) = 72π.
Estimation: round π to 3 and values to 1 s.f. to check your answer is sensible.
6-mark strategy: Step 1 draw and label; Step 2 list the parts; Step 3 find hidden lengths; Step 4 substitute into correct formulae; Step 5 combine; Step 6 units and rounding.
Show every step: M marks are awarded for method even if the arithmetic goes wrong.
Proof/'show that' questions: write the unrounded value, then the rounded value matching the target, and a concluding statement.
core.h: Links to other topics and exam strategy
core.p: 3D measure is a hub topic. It uses **Pythagoras** and **trigonometry** to find slant heights and heights, **circle** formulae for sectors and arcs, **similarity** and **area and volume scale factors** for frustums and for scaled solids, **algebra** for equal volume and 'in terms of x' questions, and **ratio** and **density** for real-life problems. Because of this, the same question may be marked partly on the geometry, partly on the algebra and partly on communication.

exam: 1 mark: a single correct substitution or conversion, for example 'r = 6' from a diameter of 12, or '1 litre = 1000 cm³'.
2 marks: substitute into the correct formula and evaluate, for example ⅓ × π × 5² × 12 = 314 cm³. Method mark for the formula with correct numbers, accuracy mark for the answer.
3 marks: usually a hidden length is needed first, for example Pythagoras to get a slant height or vertical height, then the formula.
4 marks: composite solids, with one mark per part's volume, one for adding or subtracting, and one for the correct final answer with units.
6 marks: a problem-solving chain (e.g. melted-down solid, or comparing two containers). Mark scheme: formula for each solid, set up an equation or comparison, solve, then conclude in context.
Command words: 'show that' needs the unrounded value and a conclusion; 'give your answer in terms of π' means do not use a decimal; 'work out the exact' means leave surds and π.
Always label a diagram: draw the right-angled triangle for the slant height separately and write the lengths on it.
Write the formula first, then substitute. If you slip on arithmetic, you still earn the method mark.
Check whether the question says 'open', 'closed', 'solid' or 'hollow' and include the right faces for surface area.
Estimate with π ≈ 3 to see if your answer is the right size, then do the exact calculation.
Model phrase for composite solids: 'volume of cone + volume of hemisphere' written explicitly in your working, so the examiner sees the structure.
Final line: write units and state the answer clearly, rounded to 3 s.f. when no accuracy is given.

mistakes.r: Volume uses the perpendicular height h. Slant height is only used for curved surface area (πrl) or the area of a triangular face; find h with Pythagoras if needed.
mistakes.w: Using the slant height l in the volume formula of a cone or pyramid.

mistakes.r: Always halve the diameter first. Write 'r = 6' at the start of the working.
mistakes.w: Using the diameter in place of the radius (for example r = 12 when the diameter is 12).

mistakes.r: Cones and pyramids are one third of the matching cylinder or prism. Volume of a cone = ⅓πr²h, pyramid = ⅓ × base area × h.
mistakes.w: Forgetting the ⅓ in the cone or pyramid volume formula.

mistakes.r: Volume is cm³, surface area is cm². The accuracy mark needs the correct units.
mistakes.w: Writing the answer to a volume in cm² (or an area in cm³).

mistakes.r: Only surfaces on the outside are counted. When two parts are joined, the faces in contact are hidden and are left out.
mistakes.w: Counting the glued faces in a composite solid's surface area.

mistakes.r: 2πr² is the curved surface only. The total surface area of a solid hemisphere is 2πr² + πr² = 3πr².
mistakes.w: Giving total surface area of a solid hemisphere as 2πr².

mistakes.r: Each triangular face has area ½ × base edge × slant height, where the slant height comes from Pythagoras (h² + (a/2)²).
mistakes.w: Using the vertical height for the area of a triangular face of a pyramid.

mistakes.r: Keep full calculator values (use ANS) and round only the final answer to 3 significant figures.
mistakes.w: Rounding intermediate answers (for example slant height 7.2) and losing accuracy.

mistakes.r: Convert everything to the same unit before substituting. Remember 1 m³ = 1 000 000 cm³.
mistakes.w: Mixing units, such as radius in metres and height in centimetres.

mistakes.r: Find the volume of the whole large cone, then subtract the volume of the small cone removed; use similar triangles to find the small cone's dimensions.
mistakes.w: Frustum: subtracting radii or heights instead of volumes.

summary: You must be able to calculate the volume and surface area of prisms, cylinders, pyramids, cones, spheres and hemispheres, and of composite solids and frustums built from them, giving answers in the correct units and (when asked) in terms of π. It matters because 3D measure questions appear on every Higher paper, often as multi-step 4 to 6 mark problems that also pull in Pythagoras, similarity and algebra.

terms.d: The amount of three-dimensional space occupied by a solid, measured in cubic units such as cm³.
The total area of all the faces or surfaces of a 3D shape, measured in square units such as cm².
A solid with a constant cross-section along its whole length; its volume is area of cross-section × length.
The shape you see when you cut straight through a solid, at right angles to its length.
A solid with a polygon base and triangular faces that meet at one point, the apex; volume = ⅓ × base area × perpendicular height.
The single point at the top of a pyramid or cone where the sloping faces or surface meet.
The height measured at right angles to the base, from the base up to the apex; this is the height used in volume formulae.
The length measured along the sloping surface from the apex to the edge of the base of a cone (or down the middle of a triangular face of a pyramid).
A solid with a circular base and a curved surface tapering to an apex; V = ⅓πr²h and curved surface area = πrl.
A perfectly round solid, every point on its surface a distance r from the centre; V = 4/3 πr³ and surface area = 4πr².
Half of a sphere; volume ⅔πr³, curved surface area 2πr².
A solid made by joining two or more simpler solids; hidden joined faces are not counted in the surface area.
The solid left when a smaller cone is removed from the top of a cone by a cut parallel to the base.
The volume of liquid a container can hold; 1 litre = 1000 cm³.
An exact answer written with the symbol π kept in it, for example 36π cm³, instead of a decimal.
Mass per unit volume: density = mass ÷ volume.

worked.q: A cone has base radius 5 cm and perpendicular height 12 cm. Work out (a) its volume in terms of π, (b) its total surface area to 3 significant figures. (5 marks)
steps: Total surface area = πrl + πr² = π × 5 × 13 + π × 5² = 65π + 25π (M1).

worked.q: A solid toy is made from a cone joined to a hemisphere. Both have radius 3 cm. The cone has perpendicular height 4 cm. Work out the total surface area of the toy, giving your answer to 3 significant figures. (5 marks)
steps: Slant height of the cone l = √(3² + 4²) = 5 cm (M1).
Curved surface area of cone = πrl = π × 3 × 5 = 15π (M1).
Curved surface area of hemisphere = ½ × 4πr² = 2π × 9 = 18π (M1).
The flat faces where the cone and hemisphere are joined are not on the outside so are not counted (M1).

worked.q: A square-based pyramid has base side 8 cm and perpendicular height 6 cm. Work out (a) its volume, (b) its total surface area to 3 significant figures. (6 marks)
steps: Slant height of a triangular face: l² = 6² + 4² = 36 + 16 = 52, so l = √52 = 7.211... cm (M1).
Area of one triangular face = ½ × 8 × 7.211 = 28.84 cm²; four faces = 115.38 cm² (M1).
